items.title: TN Speaker’s anti-abortion rhetoric is more than a personal opinion
items.summary: Abortion rights in India are hard-won. In 2021, the Supreme Court observed in a landmark judgement that reproductive autonomy is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution. That means a woman can choose whether or not to exercise her right to abortion. Gods of any religion and their earth-bound spokespersons have no say in women’s bodily autonomy. Yet accessing safe abortion, without judgement, remains a Herculean battle. Pro-life (anti-abortionist) noise continues to drown out the simple facts of choice and consent. Adding to that noise on August 9 were Catholic groups and Tamil Nadu Assembly Speaker JCD Prabhakar who is also the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam’s (TVK) MLA from Thousand Lights in Chennai. Speaking at an event organised by CHARIS India under the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India (CBCI), Prabhakar declared: “Life begins at conception.” This has been the tiresome slogan of anti-abortionists globally. It is the regular rallying cry of Christian nationalist Republicans in the US who seek to wipe out reproductive rights under the guise of protecting ‘all life’. The event, held at Stella Maris College, a women-only institute, was meant to coincide with the anniversary of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, passed in 1957 and amended in 2021. So far, anti-abortion sentiments have not played a major role in Tamil Nadu’s politics. Some argue that Prabhakar’s stance is his own and that it cannot be interpreted as the state government’s. Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, who keeps claiming that his government stands for women, has said nothing yet. Doubling down while speaking to the press at the event, Prabhakar said, “Various governments across the world have different views. But here, the Christian community has the strong belief that abortion should never take place at any point. Because every child is a gift from God. That gift must be cherished by every woman and every family.” He also said that the issue will be brought to Vijay’s notice, who has “innovative ideas”. items.title: The 'hands-off' doctrine in election disputes: A case for reconsideration
items.summary: Democracy, as the Supreme Court has repeatedly reminded us, is not merely an incident of our constitutional scheme, but a part of its basic structure. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu , the Supreme Court held that ‘democracy’ and ‘free and fair elections’ are inseparable twins. In Rajbala v. State of Haryana , the Supreme Court described the right to vote and right to contest in elections to local bodies as constitutional rights. Earlier, in Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal , the Supreme Court held that the said right is neither a fundamental right nor a common law right, but a statutory right. Rajbala reads it to constitutional rank at least in elections to panchayats. Nothing in this article turns on winning that classificatory battle. Constitutional right or statutory right, the interest at stake is the same and the Court’s own basic structure jurisprudence has already told us how much it weighs. Yet, when disputes touching upon the electoral process are actually brought before the constitutional courts, a curious reluctance sets in. The courts, almost as a matter of settled practice, decline to entertain such disputes and relegate the aggrieved party to the statutory remedy of an election petition. The doctrine finds its origin in NP Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer and has been consistently reaffirmed most recently in State of Goa v. Fouziya Imtiaz Shaikh , where the Supreme Court held that once the electoral process has commenced, there must be a complete hands-off approach on the part of the High Courts exercising jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, 1950. The doctrinal tension A real tension lies at the heart of this jurisprudence. If free and fair elections are indeed a basic feature of the Constitution of India and the right to vote and right to contest at least in local body elections is given constitutional character, it is difficult to reconcile this position with a rule that leaves illegalities in the electoral process wholly unaddressed by the constitutional courts until the election is over. By that time, in most cases, the term of the elected body has run its course and the grievance has become academic. The rationale for the hands-off approach is not without force. Elections must proceed without interruption and courts have been understandably reluctant to become instruments of delay in a process that is time-bound by its very nature. items.title: Hens are 'livestock' under MV Act; owner can claim insurance for loss of hens in road accident: Karnataka HC
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently held that hens constitute 'livestock' under the Motor Vehicles Act and therefore, their loss in a road accident can be treated as damage to goods covered by a motor insurance policy [K Veera Narayana Swamy vs Y Yankappa] . Justice Geetha KB rejected Reliance General Insurance Company's argument that hens cannot be considered livestock. It was dealing with the insurer's challenge against the grant of compensation of ₹4.51 lakh by a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) to a poultry farm owner after his 2,000 broiler hens died in the road accident. "Livestock means and includes hens. Hence, the hen is considered as livestock" the Court said. It relied upon Section 2(13) of Motor Vehicles Act which states that ‘goods’ include livestock. Justice Geetha KB The poultry farm owner had earlier claimed compensation of ₹5.90 lakh in connection with the death of 2,250 broiler hens that were being transported in an Eicher van. The claimant said the vehicle overturned, resulting in the death of around 2,000 hens, while the remaining 250 were allegedly taken away by people from the neighbouring area. The tribunal awarded ₹4.51 lakh with 7% annual interest. Before the High Court, the insurer contended that the claimant had failed to establish compliance with Rule 74 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 concerning transportation of cattle. It was also argued that hens could not be treated as livestock and that the insurance policy did not cover the goods in question. However, the High Court rejected the insurer's reliance on Rule 74. While the Court acknowledged that explanation to Rule 74 defines “cattle” to include goat, sheep, buffalo, bull, ox, cow, deer, horse, pony, mule, ass, pig and their young ones but not hens, it referred to Section 2(13) of the Motor Vehicles Act, which defines “goods” and includes livestock within its ambit. "In the policy under the head ‘limits of liability’, it is held that the policy is including death of or bodily injury to any person so far as it is necessary to meet the requirements of Motor Vehicles Act and policy i.e. damage to property other than property belonging to the insured or held in trust or in custody of control of the insured up to the limits of ₹7.5 lakhs," it noted. Therefore, the Court held that the claimant was transporting livestock in the offending vehicle and found no reason to interfere with the tribunal's award of ₹4.51 lakh. items.title: Supreme Court flags need for more commercial courts, seeks State-wise data on litigation trends
items.summary: Speedy resolution of commercial disputes is integral to the ease of doing business, the Supreme Court said on Monday as it flagged the need to assess whether more commercial courts are required across states. Hence, a bench of Chief Justice of India CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana proceeded to seek the latest data on the number of pending commercial cases along with the corresponding infrastructure provided to commercial courts. "The whole idea of commercial courts is to expedite the hearing... A part of ease of doing business is how fast a commercial dispute is decided by the courts," the Court said explaining the logic behind setting up commercial courts. Justice Joymalya Bagchi, CJI Surya Kant and Justice V Mohana The Court asked whether there was any evaluation of the pendency or trend of cases filed under the Commercial Courts Act. The amicus curiae informed the bench that this information has not been placed on record, though the Court's April 2025 order had specifically asked High Courts to indicate the time being taken in such matters. The Chief Justice said the requirement for additional courts would depend on the State and establishing courts in one go may not always be feasible since it depends on infrastructure and availability of officers. He said a phased, state-wise assessment was needed along with an indication of how many courts were immediately required, since long delays could not be afforded. Supreme Court, Arvind Datar Senior Advocate Arvind Datar also said that the requirement would vary from one State to another. The CJI agreed. "Some of these States have cosmopolitan or major urban cities where commercial litigation might be very high as compared to other States which are dominated by rural areas," the CJI said. The Court then proceeded to seek the latest data as on January 31, 2026 with regard to the number of pending commercial cases and the infrastructure made available to commercial courts. The Court also directed the concerned parties to collect State-wise data on the growing trend of commercial litigation and prepare an estimate of the increased litigation and the requirement for additional commercial courts in such states. items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to entertain a public interest litigation (PIL) petition seeking steps to register, recognise, supervise and monitor all institutions, imparting secular education and/or religious instructions to children up to the age of 14 years. The petition filed by BJP leader and advocate Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay also alleged that semi-religious minority educational institutions, operating the under the garb of Article 30 (right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions), are radicalising gullible children. "Presently, semi-religious minority educational institutions are being covered under Article 30, which is a wrong interpretation. Thousands of non-registered institutions are radicalising gullible young children under the garb of imparting religious instruction as they are not monitored by the State. It has serious implications not only for internal security but also fraternity, unity and national integration, as one can easily brainwash young children in the name of religion," the petition said. A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul Pancholi declined to entertain the plea prompting Upadhyay to withdraw the petition. "Petitioner seeks to withdraw his petition and pursue his remedy in appropriate forum," the Court noted. items.title: Kerala: LP school PSC rank holders end hunger strike following talks with govt
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Rank holders on the Kerala Public Service Commission’s (PSC) list for appointment to lower primary schools ended a 13-day indefinite hunger strike on Tuesday, August 11, following talks with the government. The hunger strike was part of a 37-day-long protest organised by the All Kerala Lower Primary School Teacher (LPST) PSC Rank Holders' Association. S Valarmathi, the association secretary, broke her fast by accepting a drink of water from General Education Minister N Samsudheen. The government has sought 45 days to examine the protesters' demands. “I am happy that we were able to conclude the discussions on a positive note. The hunger strike has now been called off,” said Valarmathi after the meeting with the Minister. The rank holders’ indefinite protest outside the Kerala Secretariat in Thiruvananthapuram, demanded immediate appointment orders from the May 2025 Kerala PSC rank list. They also demanded extending the validity of the rank list, as many of the rank holders on the current list have not got jobs. They also demanded a reduction in the teacher-student ratio from 1:30 to 1:25. Additionally, they demanded that the government fill Head Teacher Vacancy (HTV) posts in schools. In schools with more than 150 students, head teachers do not have to teach; instead, they can appoint another teacher to take their place, typically on a daily-wage basis. The protesters further demanded that teacher appointments to aided schools be conducted through the PSC. Currently, the government pays teacher salaries in aided institutions while appointments are made by the school managements. Minister N Shamsudheen told the media that reviewing some of the demands will require time. He stated, “Notifications and postings should align with the actual number of vacancies available. This rank list is valid for one-and-a-half years. A decision has been made to begin the procedures for further extending the validity of the list.” On head teacher vacancy appointments, he said, “Some time has been requested to examine and decide on the matter. A study should also be conducted on what could happen when the teacher-student ratio reduces to 1:25. We have requested time for that as well,” he added. The government has also assured the PSC rank holders that no one who has secured a job through the PSC rank list will lose it due to division fall, resulting from a drop in the number of students in a year.

items.title: Telangana SIR: Over 73 lakh voters marked absent, dead, shifted, or duplicate
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The enumeration forms of 2.64 crore voters in Telangana have been digitised as part of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, according to State Chief Electoral Officer C Sudarshan Reddy. The CEO’s office said on Tuesday, August 11, that 78.30% of the state’s 3.38 crore voters had their enumeration forms digitised. The update came a day after the door-to-door verification exercise by booth-level officers concluded on Monday. Around 73.39 lakh enumeration forms, or 21.70% of the total, remain undigitised and have been classified as “uncollectable”. Of these, 9.22 lakh voters have been marked as dead, while 11.25 lakh were classified as absent or untraceable. Another 45.18 lakh voters were found to have permanently shifted, while 6.70 lakh were marked as already enrolled. The CEO’s office also placed 1.02 lakh voters under the “others” category, without specifying what this classification means. Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri recorded the highest rate of digitisation in the state at 94.31%, while Hyderabad recorded the lowest at 58.89%. Under the revised SIR schedule, the draft electoral rolls will be published on August 17. Voters will be able to file claims and objections between August 17 and September 16. The process of serving notices and disposing of claims and objections will continue until October 15. The final electoral rolls are scheduled to be published on October 19. items.title: Wildlife department to probe origin of lar gibbon seen in actor Vikram’s video
items.summary: Actor Chiyaan Vikram has drawn the attention of wildlife authorities and conservationists after sharing a video of himself interacting with a lar gibbon. The species is a threatened primate protected under international wildlife trade regulations. The video, which Vikram posted on social media, showed him playing with a well-grown lar gibbon. It quickly went viral, but also triggered questions over how the exotic animal came to be in a private setting in Chennai and whether its owner possesses the documents required to legally keep it. The lar gibbon, scientifically known as Hylobates lar, is native to Southeast Asia and is listed under Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). The species is also classified as a Schedule IV animal under India's amended Wildlife Protection Act. Under CITES, Appendix I covers species facing the highest level of protection and places stringent restrictions on international commercial trade. Possession of an exotic animal in India can also be subject to domestic requirements concerning its acquisition, registration, transfer and supporting documentation. Records show the Lar Gibbons passed from Laikhuram Singh in Manipur to SK Keshavanathan in Erode, and were then sold on to Chinni Krishna Ranganathan in Chennai. Chennai wildlife warden Kulal Yogesh Vilas, speaking to Times of India, said the wildlife department would verify the animal's origin, including who it was procured from and whether the owner has documents establishing its purchase and possession. A forest ranger would be sent to conduct the verification, Yogesh Vilas said. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau also said state wildlife authorities are generally asked to examine cases involving exotic pets and verify whether owners have valid documents and details about the source of the animals. The report added that V Thenmozhi, deputy director of the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau's southern region, said authorities seek the assistance of state wildlife officials in such cases to check documentation and establish where an exotic animal was sourced. The video has also raised concerns among conservationists because of the way lar gibbons are captured and traded.
